modules.title: Order parameters, residual symmetries, and invariants
modules.summary: Automatically generate second-, fourth-, and sixth-order invariants from a  polar vector  representation of a finite  point group . Track a chosen direction's  stabilizer subgroup , parent-group orbit, external-field splitting, and coordinate conventions.

Oₕ: three-dimensional  order parameter  (x, y, z components)

predictions.question: For the two-dimensional  polar vector  of C₄ᵥ along x, how many distinct directions occur in the parent-group orbit?
predictions.explanation: The parent group has order 8 and the stabilizer of this nonzero vector has order 2, so the orbit has size 8/2=4. Not every operation produces a new direction.

predictions.question: After adding −h_xη_x to a cubic polar vector, do all six axial states in the parent-group orbit remain degenerate?
choices: Yes; the parent group is unchanged
No; the external field lowers the symmetry of the energy function
predictions.explanation: This preset has h_x=0.3, giving three energies for +x,−x, and the four directions perpendicular to x. The parent-group orbit is not the set of degenerate domains after applying the field.

predictions.question: With bond-center inversion retained, what happens to nonzero input Dx, Dy, Dz?
choices: All three D components are forbidden
DMI becomes a stronger isotropic exchange
predictions.explanation: Inversion leaves axial-spin components unchanged but exchanges the two endpoints. Thus J=J^T and the antisymmetric exchange D=0.

predictions.question: How does the two-spin spectrum change if only endpoint labels are exchanged and coordinates consistently transformed?
predictions.explanation: Transposing J and applying orthogonal similarity are equivalent to exchanging and  change of basis  of quantum spins. D components may change, but all four energies are preserved.

predictions.question: For isotropic exchange, must each exchange term separately commute with S_x?
choices: Yes; every term must vanish separately
Not necessarily; commutators from the y and z terms may cancel
There is no need to check commutators
predictions.explanation: For J_y=J_z, the two contributions cancel and the complete Hamiltonian commutes with total S_x. Sum the matrices first, then take the norm.

predictions.question: Is total S_x necessarily still conserved when local z pure dephasing is added to isotropic exchange, which preserves SU(2)?
choices: No; check the complete L†S_x as well
Choosing the singlet alone ensures conservation for every initial state
predictions.explanation: The Hamiltonian part commutes with S_x, but local z pure dephasing gives L†S_x=−γ_φ S_x; conservation for all initial states is broken.

lessons.title: From order-parameter directions to surviving operations and domains
lessons.summary: Calculate separately the symmetry of a specified state, the symmetry of its energy function, and its orbit of equivalent states.

sections.title: Specify the representation first
sections.text: In this experiment the order parameter is a two-dimensional polar vector of C₄ᵥ or a three-dimensional polar vector of O_h. Point-group matrices act on η; inversion of an O_h polar vector is −I. Oxygen-octahedron rotations are axial vectors, so this inversion rule cannot be applied directly.

sections.title: State  stabilizer subgroup
sections.text: Test D(g)η=η operation by operation; the surviving operations form the stabilizer subgroup. The zero vector preserves the parent group, while a nonzero direction can lower symmetry. Comparisons use a numerical tolerance of 1e−9, with the actual matrices generated as exact integers.

sections.title: An orbit is not an operation list
sections.text: Different operations may send η to the same direction, so duplicates must be removed. O_h generates six directions along coordinate axes and eight along body diagonals, arising from different  stabilizer subgroup . Specifying a direction alone does not prove a free-energy minimum there.

sections.title: Material connections and limitations
sections.text: Axial or diagonal BaTiO₃ polarization directions provide visual context. This tool does not automatically construct actual atomic displacements, space-group subgroups, translational domains, or experimental phase diagrams. Use the structural-distortion and phase-transition modules to study specified modes and energies.

lessons.title: Derive allowed free-energy terms using each  generator
lessons.summary: Generate independent invariants by monomial group averaging, then use actual coefficients to plot energy-surface sections.

sections.title: Start with one monomial
sections.text: Apply all group operations to monomials such as η_x² and average. Monomials canceled by signs produce no invariant; equivalent monomials give repeated orbit sums. Retain independent orbit sums, optionally normalized to minimal integer coefficients.

sections.title: Constraints have traceable origins
sections.text: Click a coefficient relation to inspect the generator matrix and the exponents and signs before and after transformation. A mirror reverses the sign of η_xη_y, forcing its coefficient to zero; a fourfold rotation requires equal coefficients for η_x² and η_y².

sections.title: Allowed forms do not determine coefficients
sections.text: C₄ᵥ has 1,2,2 independent invariants at orders two, four and six; O_h has 1,2,3. Coefficients are teaching inputs whose signs and magnitudes are not determined by symmetry. Continuous isotropy at second order can be an accidental feature of a low-order truncation.
sections.formula: F = a₂ I₂ + b₄ I₄a + c₄ I₄b + d₆ I₆a + e₆ I₆b + f₆ I₆c

sections.title: Radial minima and full stability
sections.text: Solve for every real stationary point of the one-variable polynomial along the selected direction. These are not all minima of the multidimensional free energy. The angular scan fixes the xy radius and z component; a flat curve or local minimum alone cannot establish a thermodynamic phase. Highest-order boundedness is checked using sufficient conditions, with limitations stated when they fail.

lessons.title: Explicit symmetry breaking, domain energies and coordinate conventions
lessons.summary: Distinguish physically changing an external field from passively changing coordinate notation.

sections.title: An external field does not automatically preserve the parent group
sections.text: With a fixed linear field along laboratory x, retain only operations that also preserve the field. The parent-group orbit remains useful for comparison, but its different directions may split in energy.

sections.title: Distinguishing three groups
sections.text: Inspect separately parent group G, the field-preserving energy-symmetry group G_h, and the intersection preserving both field and state. A state's  stabilizer subgroup  alone does not establish spontaneous symmetry breaking of the entire Hamiltonian.

sections.title: Passive coordinate transformation
sections.text: The columns of Q are new coordinate axes expressed in old coordinates. η, the field, group matrices and energy expression must all transform together. Rotating only the order parameter while leaving the energy anisotropy unchanged generally changes the physical state.
sections.formula: η′ = Qᵀη；D′ = Qᵀ D Q；F′(η′) = F(Qη′)

sections.title: Verify rather than compare entries one by one
sections.text: Compare energy,  stabilizer subgroup  order, and the  covariance residual  of operation actions in both coordinate systems. Matrix entries may change; energy and orbit counts are the quantities to preserve here.

lessons.title: Derive allowed exchange interactions from bond symmetry
lessons.summary: The same spatial operation not only transforms the spin component, but also exchanges the two endpoints of the bond.

sections.title: First declare the directed bond and spin convention
sections.text: Put i at (−1/2,0,0) and j at (1/2,0,0). J is a real 3×3 matrix, the quantum spin S=σ/2 is dimensionless, and the unit of all exchange coefficients is meV. Flip arrows are not a new interaction.

sections.title: spin is axial vector
sections.text: is transformed by R, and the real spin is transformed by A=det(R)R. Inversion reverses the position while maintaining the spin component; the spin cannot be treated as an ordinary displacement under the mirror.

sections.title: Endpoint exchange determines whether to transpose
sections.text: When the operation maintains two endpoints, the converted energy is given by A^TJA; when the operation switches endpoints, the spin order needs to be restored to i on the left and j on the right, so J^T appears. The interface will list every linear coefficient relationship generated by this operation.

sections.title: The conclusion and complete group of a generator
sections.text: An x-directed bond lies in the xy mirror plane, so allowed D is perpendicular to that plane. Bond-center inversion requires symmetric J and forbids all DMI. The program finds the common solution for selected generators and checks closure of the generated group. Symmetry determines the allowed space, not actual material exchange strengths.

lessons.title: Classical tilt and quantum energy levels are different issues
lessons.summary: When the same exchange matrix is applied to the unit classical arrow or spin 1/2 operator, the interpretation and normalization of the results are different.

sections.title: Decompose the exchange matrix
sections.text: The trace of J gives its isotropic part, its symmetric traceless part gives anisotropy, and its antisymmetric part corresponds to D·(Si×Sj). This site uses Jxy−Jyx=2Dz; check this sign convention before comparing references.

sections.title: Global minimum of unit classical arrow
sections.text: For two unit vectors, the lowest bilinear energy is equal to the negative value of the largest singular value of J. The left and right singular vectors give a minimal state representative; the representative is not unique when degenerate. The xy-plane exploration curve drawn in addition fixes the first spin and cannot be universally equivalent to the global minimum.

sections.title: Direct diagonalization of quantum dimers
sections.text: uses σa⊗σb/4 to construct a 4×4 matrix. When there is only isotropic antiferromagnetic J, the singlet energy is −3J/4 and the triplet energy is J/4. Classical energy −J and quantum energy −3J/4 cannot be compared equally without normalization.

sections.title: The tilted arrow is not the quantum local magnetic moment
sections.text: interface reports equal-weighted density matrix and spin correlations for degenerate subspaces of quantum ground states. The square of time reversal for two spin 1/2 ensembles is +1, and time reversal itself does not guarantee Kramers pairing; energy level degeneracy may also depend on special parameters.

lessons.title: Exchange coordinates, exchange endpoints and comparable physical results
lessons.summary: distinguishes between changing symmetry constraints, changing interactions, and only changing representation conventions.

sections.title: coordinate axis rotation adopts passive convention
sections.text: The new axis rotates θ around z relative to the old axis, and the component satisfies v′=Q^Tv. The exchange matrix transforms uniformly with the spin components on both sides; here it is an orthogonal rotation of the right-hand axes.

sections.title: Exchange endpoints of the directed bond
sections.text: After exchanging i and j, J becomes J^T and D changes sign. At the same time, the two spins in the cross product also exchange order, and the energy does not change as a result.

sections.title: Use invariant instead of component appearance comparison
sections.text: interface lists the original tensor, the transformed tensor and two sets of quantum energy levels at the same time. The matrix elements look different and the four energies, the classical minimum energy and the spin angle should be maintained. Changing the symmetry switch can actually change the model.

sections.title: Connection to material model
sections.text: One abstract bond illustrates Moriya constraints. It connects to magnon and effective-spin-resonance lessons but does not determine lattice magnetic order automatically or make a teaching D value an actual material result.

lessons.title: From continuous rotation to complete operator conservation
lessons.summary: Use generators and commutators to connect SU(2), U(1), discrete symmetries and actual dynamics.

sections.title: Noether main line and scope of this experiment
sections.text: Continuous symmetries of the action are associated with conserved quantities. This experiment uses the corresponding criterion for a finite quantum system: for a Hermitian operator Q with no explicit time dependence, conservation for every initial state is equivalent to Q commuting with the full Hamiltonian. A finite two-spin model cannot establish spontaneous symmetry breaking in the thermodynamic limit.

sections.title: from SU(2) to U(1)
sections.text: The generator of a global rotation is the sum of the two spins. Isotropic exchange commutes with all three components. XXZ retains continuous rotations about z, but generally not about x or y. A uniform longitudinal field also preserves Sz. Conservation of S² alone does not establish SU(2): the two-spin-1/2 XYZ model without a field gradient can preserve S² without preserving the three rotation generators.

sections.title: Nonconserving term contributions can cancel
sections.text: The y term and z term of isotropic exchange are not commutation with Sx respectively, but the matrix contributions of the two cancel. Simply adding the termwise norms will falsely declare a violation; clicking on the constraint source should see both the matrix and the full residuals.

sections.title: Discrete rotations are not the same condition
sections.text: A zero-field XYZ model can retain π rotations without retaining arbitrary-angle rotations generated by the same axis. A finite-angle  commutation relations  cannot directly replace the  commutation relations  of  generator . Nonconservation along all coordinate axes also does not exclude additional symmetry about an oblique axis.

lessons.title: Hamiltonian symmetry and conservation of dissipative systems
lessons.summary: distinguishes the model's operator identities, the flat trajectory of an initial state, and the effects of bath channels.

sections.title: Check the full generator
sections.text: The Lindblad master equation specifies Hamiltonian evolution together with every dissipative channel. For time-independent Q, d⟨Q⟩/dt=⟨L†Q⟩. Conservation of Q for every initial state requires the full operator L†Q to vanish.

sections.title: What does pure dephasing preserve?
sections.text: The z channel at each site in this experiment attenuates the total transverse spin, and the dissipation contribution to the total Sz is zero. If the Hamiltonian itself is commutating with Sz, then Sz remains conserved. After adding ↑→↓ relaxation, Sz is usually no longer conserved.

sections.title: A flat curve does not prove symmetry
sections.text: The maximum mixed state I/d of a closed system is invariant under any time-independent Hamiltonian. Even if [H,Sz] is not zero, its ⟨Sz⟩ is always zero. The trajectories should be compared side by side with the operator residuals before changing the initial state.

sections.title: numerical trajectory and actual physical model
sections.text: The calculation uses a constant  generator  matrix exponential and checks the trace,  Hermitian , and positive semidefiniteness. Sparse sampling may miss oscillations but should not change the physical state at a given time. A local bath does not automatically satisfy detailed balance for a real material.

lessons.title: Time-reversal protection and consistent basis transformations
lessons.summary: Use the physical antiunitary operator to identify the origin of a degeneracy, then check the invariants after a basis change.

sections.title: Specify the physical  time reversal  first
sections.text: Physical time reversal for one spin 1/2 can be written T=−iσ_yK, with square −I. Total time reversal for two distinguishable spins acts on both and squares to +I; the Kramers condition of one spin cannot be applied directly to the full system.

sections.title: Degeneracy requires its protecting conditions
sections.text: For this finite Hamiltonian without momentum labels, T²=−I and commutation of T with H guarantee Kramers pairing. A field on a single spin breaks T; scanning εSz reveals level splitting. Two-spin T²=+I alone does not imply this conclusion.

sections.title: Other origins of two-spin multiplets
sections.text: SU(2) explains the triplet degeneracy of isotropic exchange; it is not a Kramers degeneracy due to T²=+I. For other coincident numerical levels, the program reports their multiplicities without automatically calling every coincidence accidental or topologically protected.

sections.title: change of basis  must transform every object consistently
sections.text: For new basis vectors = old basis vectors × U, H, Q, ρ and every C transform as U†AU, while the antiunitary matrix transforms as U†U_T U*. The calculation compares covariance of energy levels, expectation values, evolved states and adjoint actions. A passive basis change differs from physically rotating a sample while holding the external field fixed.

exercises.title: Infer the stabilizer from six axial directions
exercises.prompt: Use the cubic-axis preset: derive first, then calculate.

steps.prompt: What is the  polar vector  inversion matrix of O_h?
steps.hint: A polar vector changes sign under inversion.
steps.explanation: Inversion maps a nonzero  polarity  vector η to −η.

steps.prompt: How many distinct axial directions can be generated from (0,0,1)?
steps.hint: Count both signs along each of three coordinate axes.
steps.explanation: The six directions are ±x, ±y, and ±z.

steps.prompt: The parent group has order 48 and the orbit has size 6. What is the stabilizer's order?
steps.hint: Use the orbit–stabilizer relation.
steps.explanation: 48/6=8; the current direction's  point group  is C₄ᵥ.

steps.prompt: Does specifying η along z already prove an equilibrium ferroelectric phase?
steps.hint: State symmetry and energy minimization are different checks.
choices: No; energy and full stability analysis are still required
It proves stability at every temperature
It is enough to see that η is nonzero
steps.explanation: Check energy, curvature, and model validity; orbit counting alone does not determine a phase diagram.

exercises.title: Use mirrors and rotations to rule out incorrect free energies
exercises.prompt: Build the allowed terms step by step for a C₄ᵥ two-dimensional polar vector.

steps.prompt: How does η_xη_y transform under the xz mirror?
steps.hint: η_x is unchanged and η_y changes sign.
steps.explanation: Thus, if this term occurs alone, its coefficient must vanish.

steps.prompt: What constraint does a fourfold rotation place on aη_x²+bη_y²?
steps.hint: The energy must be unchanged when the two terms are exchanged.
choices: Both a and b must vanish
steps.explanation: Rotation requires equal coefficients for the two quadratic terms.

steps.prompt: Which pair gives two independent fourth-order invariants?
steps.hint: Check the mirror and fourfold rotation.
choices: η_x⁴ and η_y⁴ are independently invariant
steps.explanation: Orbit sums provide two linearly independent fourth-order invariants.

steps.prompt: What does symmetry allowance of c₄ mean?
steps.hint: Allowed does not mean determined.
choices: Its value still requires a physical model or input
steps.explanation: Symmetry constraints determine the form, not numerical parameter values for a real material.

exercises.title: Distinguish field-driven changes from coordinate changes
exercises.prompt: Use the external-field preset and the general-direction coordinate-change preset.

steps.prompt: After adding −h_xη_x with h_x>0, which of ±x has lower energy?
steps.hint: Parent-group invariants agree for +x and −x, while the linear term differs.
steps.explanation: +x has negative linear field energy and lies below −x.

steps.prompt: With an external field, can all six parent-group axial states still be called degenerate domains?
steps.hint: Check each state's actual energy.
choices: No; the external field can split the parent-group orbit
Yes, because there are still 6 spatial directions
steps.explanation: Use the symmetry group of the energy function with the field included to determine symmetry-protected energy equivalence.

steps.prompt: How should the group matrices transform in the new coordinates defined by Q?
steps.hint: Substitute η=Qη′ into Dη.
steps.explanation: The order parameter and operations must change basis consistently to preserve their action.

steps.prompt: What should remain invariant under a passive coordinate change?
steps.hint: The matrix entries need not be identical.
steps.explanation: Invariant results are preserved; coordinate components and matrix entries generally change.

exercises.title: Derive step by step why bond-centered inversion forbids DMI
exercises.prompt: Retain the xy mirror containing the bond, then enable bond-center inversion. Write position transformations, spin transformations and endpoint ordering separately.

steps.prompt: spatial inversion R=−I What is the transformation matrix for axial spin?
steps.hint: Calculate det(R)R.
steps.explanation: det(−I)=−1, so A=I; the spin is axial vector .

steps.prompt: Does bond-center inversion exchange i and j?
steps.hint: The two endpoints are located at x=±1/2.
steps.explanation: Inversion swaps the two endpoints, and the output spin order needs to be rearranged to i on the left.

steps.prompt: Which matrix condition is given by constant energy?
steps.hint: A=I, but the endpoints are swapped.
steps.explanation: The inversion constraint removes the antisymmetric part and retains any real symmetric exchange matrix.

steps.prompt: What follows for the D vector?
steps.hint: D is given by the antisymmetric part of J.
choices: D=0, but symmetric exchange can still exist
D size is uniquely determined by point group
steps.explanation: Inversion prohibits DMI; it does not require isotropy or that all symmetric anisotropy also disappears.

exercises.title: From bilinear to classical tilt and quantum energy spectrum
exercises.prompt: First use J=1meV, D=0, and then load Dz=0.6meV; read the classical and quantum results respectively.

steps.prompt: For J=1 alone, what is the energy of antiparallel classical unit vectors?
steps.hint: The unit arrow dot product is −1.
steps.explanation: The energy of the classic unit arrow is J n1·n2=−1meV.

steps.prompt: Under the same J, what is the energy of the spin 1/2 quantum singlet state?
steps.hint: Si·Sj=(Stot²−Si²−Sj²)/2。
steps.explanation: has Si²=3/4 per spin and singlet state Stot²=0, so the energy is −3J/4.

steps.prompt: What is the classical global minimum energy for a two-dimensional antisymmetric block of J I plus Dz?
steps.hint: The maximum singular value of this block is sqrt(J²+Dz²).
steps.explanation: The lower bound of the unit vector bilinear form is the negative of the largest singular value.

steps.prompt: Does the classical tilt diagram prove that the quantum ground state has the same local magnetic moment?
steps.hint: Compares classical vectors to quantum ground states 〈Si〉 in density matrix .
choices: No, the quantum expectation value needs to be calculated separately
can, the arrow in the picture is the quantum expectation value
As long as the energy is negative
steps.explanation: The two are states of different models; the ground state correlation of finite quantum dimers is not equal to the classical local arrow.

exercises.title: Check DMI sign convention with endpoint swapping and pivoting
exercises.prompt: Load the convention comparison preset, first look at the exchange label, and then look at the 37° passive rotation axis.

steps.prompt: If only labels i and j are exchanged, how does the exchange matrix transform?
steps.hint: rewrites Sj^T J Si as Si on the left.
steps.explanation: Scalar interactions correspond to transposed matrices after exchanging order.

steps.prompt: How does the corresponding D vector transform?
steps.hint: Antisymmetric matrix transpose and sign change.
steps.explanation: D flip and Si×Sj flip occur simultaneously, and the physical energy remains unchanged.

steps.prompt: Press v′=Q^Tv to change coordinates. How does the matrix change?
steps.hint: Substitute the old components v=Qv′ into the bilinear form.
steps.explanation: The components on both sides must be transformed at the same time to obtain the passive coordinate formula.

steps.prompt: Which quantity best checks that this is only a convention change?
steps.hint: Don't just compare J with different coordinates element by element.
choices: Four quantum energy levels and classical minimum energy
Jxy must be equal term by term
steps.explanation: The full spectrum and scalar energy are preserved; components and the sign of D can change with conventions.

exercises.title: Check each step of symmetry breaking from SU(2) to U(1)
exercises.prompt: Compare the isotropic, XXZ, and XYZ presets in sequence, retaining coefficient units and the S=σ/2 convention.

steps.prompt: Which quantity tests conservation of Q in a closed system for every initial state?
steps.hint: Q has no explicit time dependence; check the operator identity.
steps.explanation: The guarantee for all initial states is given only if the complete commutator is zero.

steps.prompt: Must every isotropic-exchange term commute with Sx individually?
steps.hint: The norm is calculated after adding the matrices.
choices: Only necessary when the initial state is pure
steps.explanation: y and z exchange terms cancel at Jy=Jz.

steps.prompt: XXZ, Jx=Jy≠Jz has no transverse field. Which coordinate axis generator is still conserved?
steps.hint: Rotation about z mixes the x and y components.
steps.explanation: Jx=Jy preserves continuous rotation about z.

steps.prompt: XYZ retains π rotation around z, does it necessarily retain Sz?
steps.hint: Finite angle symmetry is weaker than arbitrary angle continuous symmetry.
choices: is conserved only after changing the unit to eV
steps.explanation: Discrete rotations do not automatically give continuous generator conservation.

exercises.title: Misjudgment caused by identifying a flat trajectory
exercises.prompt: Run closed XYZ dynamics first from the maximally mixed state, then add bath channels separately.

steps.prompt: The expected value of the initial state I/d of a closed system remains unchanged. Does it prove that all Q are conserved?
steps.hint: One initial state is not equal to all initial states.
choices: only proves that all spin components are conserved
steps.explanation: I/d is commutated with any H, and its special trajectory cannot replace the operator criterion.

steps.prompt: What are the conservation conditions for all initial states when there is dissipation?
steps.hint: bath channel also enters dynamics generator .
steps.explanation: Sum the adjoint actions of the Hamiltonian and every channel.

steps.prompt: What is the dissipative contribution of local z pure dephasing to total Sz?
steps.hint: σz is commutated with the z measurement operator.
steps.explanation: This channel preserves z populations; also check whether the Hamiltonian commutes with Sz.

steps.prompt: After adding ↑→↓ relaxation, can the conservation conclusion for pure dephasing alone still be used?
steps.hint: channel change means L† change.
choices: As long as the energy is degenerate, it can
steps.explanation: Relaxation usually changes Sz and cannot be inferred from the old Hamiltonian symmetry alone.

exercises.title: distinguishes between Kramers pairing, SU(2) multiplet and change of basis
exercises.prompt: compares single spin without field, single spin with added field and isotropic double spin.

steps.prompt: What is the physics of single spin 1/2 T²?
steps.hint: T contains complex conjugation , you cannot just calculate U_T² and ignore K.
steps.explanation: T²=U_TU_T*=−I。

steps.prompt: What are two distinguishable spin 1/2 ensembles T²?
steps.hint: Total T acts on both spins.
choices: Depends on choosing the x or z basis
steps.explanation: The multiplication of two negative signs is positive, and the whole is not forced to be paired by the Kramers theorem.

steps.prompt: What can explain the triplet degeneracy of isotropically exchanged double spins?
steps.hint: examines three total spin components.
choices: Numerical solver must generate triple roots
steps.explanation: SU(2) relates different components of the same total spin multiplet .

steps.prompt: is passive and change of basis only changes H but does not change ρ and Q, can the same physical expectation be compared?
steps.hint: The same U must be used for states, operators, and dissipation channels.
choices: As long as the matrix dimension is maintained
steps.explanation: Under consistent transformations, spectra and expectations agree and L† transforms covariantly. Inconsistent transformations change the physical problem described.

cases.title: Cubic  polarity   order parameter  and ferroelectric domain directions
cases.summary: Compare residual point groups and orbit sizes for a cubic polar vector along an axis, face diagonal, and body diagonal, then connect them to a specified structural distortion.
cases.assumption: Only the polarization-direction  point group  picture is used. No BaTiO₃ parameters are fitted, and no material-specific temperature sequence, atomic modes, or complete  space group  are derived.

cases.title: In-plane ordering directions in a fourfold environment
cases.summary: At a fixed order-parameter length, compare axial and diagonal energies and examine fourth- and sixth-order anisotropy.
cases.assumption: An abstract C₄ᵥ two-dimensional polar vector does not automatically describe arbitrary surface magnetic order; axial magnetic order requires a newly specified representation.

cases.title: Field selection and one experiment in two coordinate systems
cases.kind: Explicit symmetry breaking and convention comparisons
cases.summary: Select a direction with an external field, then rotate the vector, field, operations, and energy consistently to distinguish physical changes from coordinate changes.
cases.assumption: Uniform  order parameter  and an illustrative linear field, without  domain wall  motion, hysteresis dynamics, physical electric-field units, or inversion of measured data.

cases.title: Centrosymmetric magnetic dimers: boundaries between prohibited and allowed
cases.summary: Starting from the non-zero candidate D, the bond center inversion is added, and the antisymmetric exchange is removed by observing one by one.
cases.assumption: abstracts double spin bonds and does not fit specific materials; center inversion only prohibits DMI and does not guarantee exchange isotropy.
links: Hubbard dimer and low energy spin

cases.title: D direction allowed after the ligand environment changes
cases.summary: Compare a mirror containing the bond with one perpendicular to it, distinguishing axial-vector transformations from endpoint exchange.
cases.assumption: are ideal local symmetries of the input, and no switching paths were extracted from any CIF; the size of D in the figure is not a first-principles prediction.

cases.title: Why do the two exchange parameter tables look different?
cases.summary: Change the coordinates and endpoint labels on the same dimer, and use quantum energy spectroscopy to verify that they describe the same physical interaction.
cases.assumption: only contains right-handed coordinate orthogonal rotations and endpoint exchanges; does not handle arbitrary local rotation specifications, space group standard set transformations, or material fitting.

cases.title: Molecular magnet dimers: exchange symmetry and conservation
cases.summary: Start from low-energy effective exchange, compare the conserved quantities of SU(2) and XXZ models, then relate them to a Hubbard dimer.
cases.assumption: Two effective spins and teaching coefficients; no automatic fitting exchange from structure, finite dimers do not represent long-range magnetic order.

cases.title: Same exchange Hamiltonian, different environment channels
cases.summary: maintains the exchange parameters and compares the complete conservation conditions of the closed system and the local pure decoherence with the actual trajectory.
cases.assumption: Phenomenological Markov channel, does not directly derive from lattice symmetry decoherence rate, does not simulate non-Markov bath.

cases.title: single spin time reversal protection and outfield breach
cases.summary: Start with T²=−I, introduce a controlled external field, then compare with T²=+I for two spins and with SU(2) multiplets.
cases.assumption: only diagnoses the specified finite spin space, without crystal momentum; the results are not directly extrapolated to the energy bands of all k points.
